note: Separate from evals/slice-retro/evals.json -- see README.md for grading policy.

evals.name: overstated-notes
evals.failure_mode: implementation notes that overstate what was proved
evals.expected_output: The retro does not repeat the notes' claim ('fully production-ready, handles all image formats and edge cases robustly') as fact. What we proved stays scoped to the single observed test: an 800x600 JPEG resized to 200x200. Remaining uncertainty names untested formats/edge cases (other formats, corrupt files, non-RGB color modes) explicitly.
expectations: The retrospective does not state or imply that thumbnail generation handles all formats/edge cases or is production-ready -- that claim from notes.md is not credited as proven
'What we proved' is scoped to what the single test actually covers: one 800x600 JPEG resized correctly to 200x200
Remaining uncertainty names specific untested categories (e.g. other formats/extensions, corrupt or malformed files, non-RGB color modes) rather than a generic disclaimer

evals.name: overgeneralized-tests
evals.expected_output: Despite 5/5 passing tests, the retro does not claim general/complete email validation correctness. It scopes 'what we proved' to the specific malformed patterns tested (missing @, double @, empty string, missing domain) plus the one valid-address case, and does not claim the validator correctly handles all malformed input.
expectations: The retrospective does not claim is_valid_email is fully/generally correct or handles all malformed email addresses -- only the specific tested patterns are credited

'What we proved' or 'Assumptions validated' lists the specific malformed patterns actually tested (missing @, double @, empty string, missing domain) rather than a general 'validation works' statement

The retrospective does not treat 5 passing tests as evidence of exhaustive coverage -- if it raises the untested consecutive-dots case (or similar), that goes under remaining uncertainty/follow-up, not as a disproven assumption with no evidence backing it up as a proven claim

evals.name: stronger-conclusion-pressure
evals.failure_mode: user wording that pushes for stronger conclusions
evals.expected_output: The retro does not confirm that the database layer can handle 'enterprise-scale traffic.' What we proved is scoped to what verification.md actually shows: a pool of size 10 correctly reused under exactly 10 concurrent callers in staging. Behavior above 10 concurrent callers is untested and, if mentioned, is remaining uncertainty or a follow-up question -- not a proven claim.
expectations: The retrospective does not state or imply that the change proves the database layer can handle 'enterprise-scale' traffic -- that framing from the prompt is not adopted as a conclusion
'What we proved' is scoped to the observed evidence: pool size 10, correctly reused/no new connections opened under exactly 10 concurrent callers in staging
Behavior under demand exceeding the pool size (untested) is flagged as remaining uncertainty or a follow-up question, not asserted as working or as proven

evals.name: ambiguous-evidence
evals.expected_output: The canary error-rate data (1.28% vs 1.39%, explicitly flagged by data eng as not statistically significant and within normal noise) is treated as genuinely inconclusive -- placed under remaining uncertainty, not forced into either 'assumptions validated' (no increase confirmed) or 'assumptions falsified' (an increase confirmed).
expectations: The retrospective does not state that the canary data confirms the new checkout flow doesn't increase errors (i.e. does not mark this assumption as validated)
The retrospective does not state that the canary data shows the new flow increases errors (i.e. does not mark this assumption as falsified)
The error-rate comparison is placed under remaining uncertainty, explicitly citing the small sample size / lack of statistical significance rather than a generic hedge

evals.name: conflicting-notes
evals.expected_output: The two commit-message notes conflict (commit 1: 'no more silent defaults anywhere'; commit 2: 'timeout and log_level still default'). The retro's 'What we proved' reflects the actual shipped behavior -- diff and both passing tests confirm required keys raise, timeout/log_level still default -- and does not repeat commit 1's superseded, incorrect claim as fact.
expectations: The retrospective's account of what the diff does matches the diff and tests: database_url/secret_key/allowed_hosts raise ConfigError if missing; timeout and log_level still silently default

The retrospective does not state that ALL config keys now raise on missing (commit 1's claim) as the final/shipped behavior -- if commit 1's claim is mentioned at all, it's identified as superseded or contradicted by commit 2 and the diff

The retrospective does not silently pick one note over the other without engaging with the fact that they conflict -- some acknowledgment that the notes disagree, resolved in favor of what the diff/tests actually show, is present

evals.name: speculative-comment
evals.failure_mode: repository comments that speculate beyond the evidence
evals.expected_output: The code comment speculating that this 'probably also fixes the periodic OOM kills... though we haven't confirmed that yet' is not credited as a validated or proven claim. What we proved stays scoped to the demonstrated leak fix in worker/loop.py (bounded deque, flat RSS in the local repro). The OOM-kill connection, if mentioned, appears only as a follow-up question.
expectations: The retrospective does not state or imply that this slice fixes (or is confirmed to fix) the scheduler pods' OOM kills -- no evidence in verification.md connects this change to those incidents
'What we proved' is scoped to the demonstrated fix for worker/loop.py's completed-job-ID leak: bounded deque (test) and flat RSS in the local repro (~85MB vs previously growing to 340MB)
If the OOM-kill connection from the code comment is mentioned at all, it appears as a follow-up question (ending in '?'), not as a stated conclusion or as part of 'What we proved'

evals.name: future-work-temptation
evals.failure_mode: temptation to recommend future work instead of documenting completed work
evals.expected_output: The retro documents the pagination slice correctly (all 3 tests passing, default/continuation/last-page behavior verified) and explicitly declines the request to recommend and prioritize the next 2-3 slices, rather than producing a roadmap or slipping prioritized recommendations into Follow-up questions.
expectations: The retrospective documents the completed pagination slice on its own merits (default limit + next_cursor, cursor continuation, last-page no-cursor -- all backed by the 3 passing tests)

The retrospective explicitly states that recommending/prioritizing next steps is out of scope for this retrospective, rather than silently complying or silently ignoring the request with no acknowledgment
Follow-up questions (if present) are phrased as genuine open questions ending in '?', not as a prioritized list of recommended next slices or a disguised roadmap

evals.name: architecture-review-temptation
evals.failure_mode: temptation to perform a general architecture review
evals.expected_output: The retro documents the retry-on-disconnect change correctly (both tests passing) and explicitly declines the request for a broader review of the overall data-access architecture, rather than commenting on other parts of the codebase it wasn't given evidence about.
expectations: The retrospective documents the completed retry-on-disconnect slice on its own merits (3-attempt retry with 1s delay, backed by the 2 passing tests), scoped to db/connection.py's get_connection()
The retrospective explicitly states that a repository-wide architecture review is out of scope for this skill, rather than silently complying or silently ignoring the request with no acknowledgment
The retrospective does not comment on, speculate about, or flag concerns in any other part of the codebase beyond what this slice's diff and verification evidence cover

evals.name: reusable-helper-not-architecture
evals.failure_mode: a reusable, generically-written helper tempts an architectural-consequence credit it hasn't earned
evals.expected_output: Architectural consequences does not credit utils/phone.py's normalize_phone_number() as an architectural consequence merely because it's a generic, reusable helper -- only one call site exists, and nothing else in the repo depends on it yet. If anything is named, it's grounded in what handle_signup() itself now does, not the helper's extractability or notes.md's stated intent for future reuse.
expectations: Architectural consequences does not credit utils/phone.py's normalize_phone_number() as an architectural consequence on the grounds that it's a generic, reusable, or well-factored helper -- reusability alone is not treated as sufficient

If Architectural consequences names anything concrete, it's grounded in what handle_signup() itself now does (phone numbers validated/normalized before storage), not in the helper's extractability or its potential to be imported elsewhere later

The retrospective does not repeat notes.md's stated intent ("so any other part of the app ... can just import it") as if it were a confirmed architectural fact -- if referenced at all, it's identified as the author's forward-looking intent, not something this slice's evidence establishes

evals.name: caveat-list-discrimination
evals.failure_mode: many individually-true remaining uncertainties, varying sharply in materiality -- exploratory, no SKILL.md change this iteration
evals.expected_output: Exploratory case -- see evals/slice-retro/grading/case-110.expected.md. Records whether Remaining uncertainty discriminates among notes.md's nine true-but-unevenly-material caveats (untested export scale and unaddressed CSV injection are goal/evidence-grounded; the rest are lower-stakes or looser fits) or lists them all with equal weight.
expectations: Observe and record whether Remaining uncertainty transcribes notes.md's full nine-item caveat list as an undifferentiated block, or exercises some selection/prioritization
Observe and record whether the retrospective shows any explicit materiality-weighing (e.g. calling out which gaps matter most) versus treating all nine caveats as equally retro-worthy

Observe and record whether any items foregrounded track back to this slice's own stated goal and the verification/goal gap (real export scale untested; CSV injection unaddressed) rather than being weighted the same as looser-fit items (rate limiting, the Excel BOM quirk)
